newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bundebank holds policy, but adds fresh twist.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bundebank holds policy, but adds fresh twist.

text.p: The Bundesbank on Thursday kept its monetary policy on hold, in line with expectations, but also dropped a subtle hint to financial markets that it could swing into action rapidly if a policy change was needed.

The central bank left both the growth target for its main monetary policy indicator, M3 money supply, and all of its leading interest rates unchanged at the meeting, where the main item on the agenda was a review of its M3 growth target.

Yet, apparently wary of giving the impression the powerful central bank would have its hands tied during its four-week summer break, the Bundesbank kept markets guessing as to where its main money market rate would be set in two weeks' time.

Announcing unchanged levels for the 2.50 percent discount rate and 4.50 percent discount rate, the central bank said its securities repurchase money market rate would be held at its current level of three percent for at least the next two weeks.
But it made no comment on where the so-called repo rate, which has been held steady since August, would be during the second half of the holiday period.

Although this was no cause for alarm in itself, it marked a break with tradition. In the past, during periods when the central bank has kept a close rein on its repo, the Bundesbank has usually set the rate for the whole holiday in advance.

The bank also drummed home that it was paying close attention to developments on financial markets, where German shares have soared 50 percent this year and the German currency, the mark, has lost 20 percent against the dollar.
"As in the past, the Deutsche Bundesbank will check signals emanating from the development of the money supply in the context of a broad analysis of all data relevant to prices.
"In doing this it will pay special attention to the external value of the deutschemark and events on the financial markets alongside data from the real sector," a statement said.
Analysts interpreted the Bundesbank's comments and decision as a subtle warning that while the bank saw no reason to take action now, it could do so at any time -- even over the summer.

In advance of the meeting, rumours had circulated in financial markets that the central bank could consider nudging the repo rate higher to break the strong upward trend for the dollar and share prices -- which could ultimately prove inflationary.
July inflation figures released on Thursday showed annual inflation creeping up to 1.8 percent from 1.7 percent.

Juergen Pfister, senior economist at Commerzbank in Frankfurt said the decision to say nothing on the further outlook for the repo rate was by no means a clue that an increase in the rate was on the cards.
But he added, "They have given themselves a little escape clause due to the developments on the exchange markets. That means they could act if the mark continued to weaken further."

Thomas Mayer, senior economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt, agreed. "I suppose it is a subtle message -- we will see whether the market takes it as such. Often the assumption is that the Bundesbank closes down over the summer," he said.

The central policy decision to leave the M3 growth target at 3-1/2 to 6-1/2 percent for 1997 and seek expansion of around five percent in the aggregate through 1998 was in line with analysts' expectations.

Annualised monthly M3 money supply figures, which had been consistently above the target in the first five months of this year, dropped neatly into the target range in June with growth of 6.4 percent.
The central bank said a further easing in growth was necessary for monetary policy stability, but gave no sign that there was any great cause for concern.
"By deciding to maintain its money supply target the Bundesbank is underlining that it continues to regard the money supply M3 as the central guide for monetary policy," it said.
